name: Grade 10
theme: The Church: history, mission and the Paschal Mystery lived

lessons.title: Christ founds the Church
lessons.idea: Jesus founded the Church by preaching the Kingdom, gathering disciples, choosing the Twelve, giving Peter the keys, instituting the Eucharist and sending the apostles on mission. The Church is at once a visible society and a spiritual communion.
lessons.question: What evidence shows Jesus founded a Church?
lessons.activity: “Founding evidence” (35 min). Students gather founding signs from the Gospels: the call of the Twelve (Mark 3:13–19), the keys (Matthew 16:13–20), the power to bind and loose (Matthew 18:18), the Eucharist (Luke 22:19), the commission (Matthew 28:16–20), the gift of the Spirit (John 20:21–23). Place them on a timeline and add what each shows about structure.
teach: The Church’s origin is Christ’s own work: his preaching, the call of the Twelve, the Eucharist, the Cross and the outpouring of the Spirit (CCC 758–766). She is “born from the pierced side of Christ” (CCC 766).
Matthew 16:13–20: Peter’s confession, the rock, the keys (CCC 551–553). Matthew 28:16–20: the Great Commission and the promise “I am with you always” (CCC 861).
The Church is “one complex reality” comprised of a human and a divine element (CCC 771; Lumen Gentium 8). She is a visible society and a spiritual community.
Respond to the claim “Jesus preached the Kingdom, not the Church” by showing that the Kingdom begins in the Church (CCC 541, 763–769).
talk: What evidence shows Jesus founded a community?
What is the role of the Twelve?
Why does the Church need both structure and Spirit?
quiz: Jesus called…|Twelve apostles|Seven apostles|A hundred|None|0|Mark 3:14.
The Church is…|Only spiritual|Both visible and spiritual|A private club|Only an institution|1|CCC 771.
The Church began…|In 1054|In Jesus’s ministry and was manifested at Pentecost|At Constantine|At Nicaea|1|CCC 763.
lessons.life: Read Matthew 16 and Acts 2 and make a two-column note: Christ’s intention / Pentecost.
lessons.saint: Peter: a fisherman who denied Jesus and was forgiven, and became the first pope.
misc: “Jesus never meant to found an organization.”
lessons.mem: “I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.” (Matthew 16:18)
lessons.hook: Ask: “If a movement lasted 2,000 years, what must have been built into it at the start?” Make a list: leaders, a mission, a way of worship, a way to hand it on.
lessons.assess: Ask students to list four New Testament actions of Jesus that show he founded a Church.

lessons.title: The Church as mystery and sacrament
lessons.idea: Vatican II calls the Church “a kind of sacrament,” a sign and instrument of communion with God and of the unity of the human race. Like the sacraments, the Church is visible and invisible at once, a mystery rooted in the Trinity.
lessons.question: What does “sacrament of salvation” mean?
lessons.activity: “Read Lumen Gentium 1” (35 min). Students read the opening paragraph of Lumen Gentium and annotate: “sacrament,” “sign,” “instrument,” “union with God,” “unity of the whole human race.” Then write a paragraph explaining in plain words what it means that the Church is a sacrament, giving one example. Read Ephesians 5:25–32.
teach: The Church is the “universal sacrament of salvation” (CCC 774–776). She is the sign that points to Christ and the instrument through which he works.
“Mystery” (mysterion) in Ephesians means God’s hidden plan revealed in Christ (CCC 770–773). The Church is also the “bride” for whom Christ gave himself.
She originates in the Trinity: People of God of the Father, Body of Christ the Son, Temple of the Spirit (CCC 781–810).
This reading avoids two errors: the Church as a purely human institution, or as invisibly pure with no human structure.
talk: How is the Church a sacrament?
What is the difference between sign and instrument?
What does this say about her failings?
quiz: The Church is a sacrament in the sense that she is…|Sign and instrument of union with God|One of the seven|Only a ritual|Only a building|0|CCC 775.
Mystery means…|Secret|Puzzle|Hidden reality visible in signs|Impossibility|2|CCC 770.
Lumen Gentium means…|Joy and hope|Light of the nations|Word of God|Dogmatic constitution|1|Vatican II.
lessons.life: Read Lumen Gentium 1–8.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Siena: a lay Dominican who counseled popes and loved the Church while calling for reform.
misc: “Sacrament” means the Church has the same status as Baptism.
lessons.mem: “The church is, in Christ, a kind of sacrament — a sign and instrument of communion with God and of unity among all men.” (Lumen Gentium 1)
lessons.hook: Show a wedding ring. “What does it do? It points to love and also helps create it.” A sacrament does the same thing, and the Church is the sacrament of Christ.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain in their own words why the Church is called a sacrament.

lessons.title: People of God, Body of Christ, Temple of the Spirit
lessons.idea: Three biblical images describe the Church. She is the People of God (a priestly, prophetic, royal people), the Body of Christ (head and members, nourished by the Eucharist) and the Temple of the Holy Spirit (the Spirit as her soul).
lessons.question: Which image is most helpful?
lessons.activity: “Illustrate the three images” (35 min). Groups make an infographic for one image with: Scripture (1 Peter 2:9–10; 1 Corinthians 12:12–27; 1 Corinthians 3:16–17), meaning, consequences for how we live, and a modern example (parish, Eucharist, Spirit). Present and combine into a class booklet.
teach: People of God (CCC 781–786): chosen, redeemed, priestly, prophetic, kingly; the law is love. Body of Christ (CCC 787–795): Christ is head; Baptism and the Eucharist make us one body. Temple of the Spirit (CCC 797–801): the Spirit gives life, unity and charisms.
Together these correct each other: People of God stresses history and pilgrimage; Body, intimacy and unity; Temple, holiness.
Pope Pius XII’s Mystici Corporis (1943) is a classic text on the Body. Vatican II gave priority to People of God.
Ask students which image speaks to them now.
quiz: The Body of Christ emphasizes…|Union with Christ|Rank|Rules|Politics|0|CCC 789.
The Church is the Temple of…|The Holy Spirit|Peter|Rome|Solomon|0|CCC 797.
People of God emphasizes…|Common dignity of baptism|Only clergy|Only laity|Rank|0|CCC 782.
lessons.life: Illustrate three images.
lessons.saint: Paul: once a persecutor, he met Christ on the road to Damascus and became the apostle to the Gentiles.
misc: “People of God means the Church is a democracy.”
“The Body of Christ is only a metaphor.”
lessons.mem: “Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it.” (1 Corinthians 12:27)
lessons.hook: Show three objects: a team jersey, a body model, a temple model. “Each says something different about belonging.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain each image and what it implies for parish life.

units.title: Marks and structure of the Church
units.eq: What does the Church look like?

lessons.title: One and holy
lessons.idea: The Church is one — in faith, sacraments and apostolic governance — and holy because Christ and the Spirit make her so. Divisions among Christians wound unity, and the Church works and prays for reunion.
lessons.question: Why is unity hard?
lessons.activity: “Discuss ecumenism” (35 min). A structured discussion: What unites Christians (Baptism, Scripture, the Creed)? What divides us (authority, sacraments, ministry)? What can we do (pray, study, serve together)? Review the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. Each student proposes a concrete step.
teach: The Church’s unity rests on one faith, shared sacramental life and apostolic succession (CCC 813–816). Unity is not uniformity: many rites and cultures coexist (CCC 814).
Holiness: the Church is holy because she is Christ’s Body, her means (Word and sacraments) are holy and the saints show her fruit; yet her members are sinners (CCC 823–829).

The Catholic Church works for Christian unity through prayer, dialogue and cooperation (CCC 820–822; Unitatis Redintegratio). The Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant communities differ in different degrees.
Name false irenicism: unity does not come by ignoring differences.
talk: How is the Church one yet divided?
How is she holy yet sinful?
quiz: The Church’s holiness comes from…|Her members|Her buildings|Christ|Her wealth|2|CCC 823.
Divisions among Christians…|Are unimportant|Are impossible|Are God’s plan|Contradict Christ’s will|3|CCC 817.
Unity of the Church is rooted in…|The Trinity|Law|Culture|Language|0|CCC 813.
lessons.life: Pray daily for Christian unity.
lessons.saint: John XXIII: the joyful pope who called the Second Vatican Council.
lessons.mem: “That they may all be one… so that the world may believe that you have sent me.” (John 17:21)
lessons.hook: Read John 17:20–23, Jesus’ prayer for unity. Ask: “Why does he link our unity with the world’s belief?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain unity and holiness and propose one ecumenical action.

lessons.title: Catholic and apostolic
lessons.idea: The Church is catholic: she has the fullness of faith and the means of salvation, and is sent to all peoples. She is apostolic: founded on the apostles, preserving their teaching, and led by their successors, the bishops.
lessons.question: What is apostolic succession?
lessons.activity: “Trace a bishop’s lineage” (35 min). Using apostolic succession charts, students trace their own bishop’s line of ordination back through earlier bishops (many dioceses publish this). Mark the link to the apostles. Discuss why apostolic succession matters (teaching, sacraments, unity).
teach: Catholic in two senses: the Church possesses the fullness of the means of salvation, and she is sent to the whole human race (CCC 830–831).
Apostolic: built on the foundation of the apostles (Ephesians 2:20), with their teaching kept by their successors (CCC 857–860). Bishops hand on their office by laying on of hands (CCC 861–862).
Irenaeus (c. 180) lists the bishops of Rome as proof of apostolic faith. Succession guarantees continuity of teaching and sacraments.
Distinguish “universal” from “Roman”: the Church includes Latin and Eastern rites.
quiz: “Catholic” means…|According to the whole|Local|Old|Roman|0|CCC 830.
Apostolic succession is…|Bishops receiving authority from apostles|Hereditary priests|Popular election|Tradition of music|0|CCC 861.
Clement wrote to…|Antioch|Rome|Corinth|Alexandria|2|History.
lessons.life: Find your bishop’s line of succession on a diocesan page.
lessons.saint: Ignatius of Antioch: a bishop who was thrown to the lions in Rome and wrote letters on the Eucharist and the Church.
lessons.mem: “You will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does ‘catholic’ mean?” (universal). Read Acts 1:8 and trace from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain two senses of “catholic” and what apostolic succession ensures.

lessons.title: Hierarchy and laity
lessons.idea: The Church has a hierarchical structure — Pope, bishops, priests, deacons — and a vast laity, along with consecrated life. All have different roles but share equal dignity as baptized members and the call to holiness.
lessons.question: What is the role of the laity?
lessons.activity: “Interview people in ministry” (40 min). Students prepare questions and interview (in person or by recorded interview) a priest, deacon, religious sister or brother, a lay catechist or parish worker. Ask: how they were called, what their day looks like, joys and challenges. Present insights.
teach: The hierarchy exists to serve: the Pope is the visible head of the college of bishops (CCC 880–882); bishops teach, sanctify and govern (CCC 888–896); priests are co-workers with the bishop (CCC 1562–1568); deacons serve (CCC 1569–1571).
The laity share in Christ’s priestly, prophetic and kingly office and have a special mission to sanctify the world from within (CCC 897–913).
Consecrated life — the evangelical counsels lived in community or alone — is a gift to the Church (CCC 914–933).
Equal dignity, different functions (CCC 872). Clericalism and passivity are both distortions.
talk: What is the role of the laity?
quiz: The laity’s distinct mission is…|To preach in Mass|To hide|To sanctify the temporal order|To rule|2|CCC 898.
Bishops are successors of…|The scribes|The apostles|The kings|The prophets|1|CCC 861.
Consecrated life is…|A gift to the Church|Invented|Dangerous|Required|0|CCC 916.
lessons.life: Interview a layperson in ministry.
lessons.saint: Josemaria: a priest who taught that ordinary work, done for love, can make us holy.
misc: “Priests and nuns are holier by nature.”
lessons.mem: “And he gave some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists, some as pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for the work of ministry.” (Ephesians 4:11–12)
lessons.hook: Read Ephesians 4:11–16. Ask: “Why does Paul say ‘to equip the saints’? Who does the work of ministry?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the roles of hierarchy, laity and consecrated life.

units.title: Church history I: the early Church

lessons.title: Pentecost to Constantine
lessons.idea: From Pentecost to Constantine the Church grew through persecution. Martyrs such as Stephen, Ignatius, Polycarp, Perpetua and Felicity bore witness, and by 313 Christians were free to worship. “The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church.”
lessons.question: Why did persecution fail?
lessons.activity: “Read martyr acts” (35 min). Groups read short excerpts from the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the Letter to the Romans by Ignatius and the Passion of Perpetua. Each group answers: What were they accused of? What did they say? What kept them going? What does this say about faith?
teach: The Church spread across the Roman Empire amid sporadic and later systematic persecution (Nero, Decius, Diocletian). Christians refused to offer incense to the emperor (CCC 2473–2474).
The early Church’s distinguishing features: Eucharist on Sunday, care for the poor, rejection of abortion and infanticide, fidelity in marriage (Didache, Justin Martyr).
In 313 Constantine and Licinius issued the Edict of Milan, granting freedom to Christians. Theodosius made Christianity the empire’s religion in 380.
Mention modern martyrs and the witness of persecuted Christians today.
quiz: The Roman charge against Christians included…|Piracy|Idolatry|Atheism|Theft|2|History.
Polycarp was bishop of…|Rome|Alexandria|Smyrna|Antioch|2|History.
The martyrs’ witness led to…|Division|Defeat|Silence|Church growth|3|Tertullian.
lessons.life: Read the Martyrdom of Polycarp.
lessons.saint: Polycarp: the aged bishop of Smyrna who died a martyr, saying, “Eighty-six years I have served him.”
lessons.mem: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life.” (Revelation 2:10)
lessons.hook: Read Revelation 2:10: “Be faithful unto death.” Ask: “What would make someone say that and mean it?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe how the early Church grew and the witness of two martyrs.

lessons.title: The Councils and the Creeds
lessons.idea: The first ecumenical councils defined who Christ and the Holy Spirit are: Nicaea (325) taught that the Son is consubstantial with the Father, Constantinople I (381) the divinity of the Spirit, Ephesus (431) that Mary is Theotokos, Chalcedon (451) the two natures of Christ.
lessons.question: What did Nicaea decide and why?
lessons.activity: “Study Arianism” (35 min). Students compare Arius’ claim (“there was when he was not”) and Athanasius’ reply with texts from John 1, John 10:30, Colossians 1:15–20. Then trace how the Nicene Creed responded. Discuss: why does it matter if Christ is God for our salvation?
teach: Arianism taught that the Son was the first and greatest creature, not eternal and not of the same being as the Father. Nicaea defined him “consubstantial” (homoousios) with the Father (CCC 242, 465).
Constantinople I affirmed the divinity of the Holy Spirit and completed the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed. Ephesus declared Mary Theotokos; Chalcedon taught one Person in two natures (CCC 466–469).
Athanasius: only God can save, so the Savior must be God (On the Incarnation). Doctrinal clarity is a service to love.
The councils’ authority comes from their reception by the Church and confirmation by the Pope.
quiz: Homoousios means…|Created|Lesser|Similar|Of one substance|3|CCC 465.
Nicaea condemned…|Monophysitism|Arianism|Gnosticism|Nestorianism|1|CCC 465.
The Nicene Creed was completed at…|Ephesus|Constantinople I|Trent|Vatican I|1|CCC 195.
lessons.life: Compare the Nicene Creed with the Apostles’ Creed.
lessons.saint: Athanasius: bishop of Alexandria, who defended the divinity of Christ through repeated exiles.
misc: “Councils voted on whether Jesus was God.”
lessons.mem: “We believe in one Lord, Jesus Christ… God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, consubstantial with the Father.” (Nicene Creed)
lessons.hook: Read John 1:1–3. Ask: “Was the Word created, or was he always?” Introduce Arius’ answer and why it mattered.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Arianism, the Nicene response and why it matters for salvation.

lessons.title: The Church Fathers
lessons.idea: The Fathers of the Church — Ignatius, Justin, Irenaeus, Athanasius, Basil, Gregory, Chrysostom, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine — handed on the apostolic faith, defended it against heresy, and wrote commentaries, sermons and treatises that still guide us.
lessons.question: What do the Fathers teach us?
lessons.activity: “Read a Father” (35 min). Students choose an excerpt from Ignatius (Smyrnaeans 6–7, on the Eucharist), Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3, on succession) or Augustine (Confessions 8, his conversion). They summarize, note the context, and write one sentence on what it teaches about the faith.
teach: The Fathers are witnesses to Tradition (CCC 11, 78, 688, 2651). Criteria for a Father: antiquity, orthodoxy, holiness, Church approval.
Greek Fathers: Athanasius, the Cappadocians (Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa), John Chrysostom. Latin Fathers: Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Gregory the Great.
Their method: read Scripture with the Church, defend the faith, form believers. Their agreement (consensus patrum) is significant.
Include women who shaped the age: Monica, Macrina, Paula.
quiz: A Father of the Church is…|A king|A priest|An early orthodox teacher|A bishop only|2|CCC 11.
Irenaeus wrote against…|Muslims|Protestants|Gnostics|Arians|2|History.
Augustine was bishop of…|Milan|Rome|Hippo|Antioch|2|History.
lessons.life: Read from Athanasius’s On the Incarnation.
lessons.saint: Athanasius: bishop of Alexandria, who defended the divinity of Christ through repeated exiles.
misc: “The Fathers are only relevant to scholars.”
lessons.mem: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” (Acts 2:42)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Who was the first to put into words something you believe?” Introduce the Fathers as the Church’s early teachers.
lessons.assess: Ask students to name three Fathers, one contribution each and why they matter.

units.title: Church history II: Middle Ages to modernity

lessons.title: Monasticism and mission
lessons.idea: Monasticism began in the desert with Anthony and Pachomius, and Benedict gave it a lasting form. Monks and missionaries such as Columban, Boniface and Cyril and Methodius evangelized Europe, copied manuscripts and built culture.
lessons.question: How did monasteries shape Europe?
lessons.activity: “Present on Benedict or Boniface” (40 min). Students prepare a five-minute presentation on a monk or missionary: context, work, quote, legacy. Include maps. Class feedback: what does this witness teach about faith and culture?
teach: Monasticism (CCC 918–927): from the hermits of Egypt (Anthony c. 270) to communities (Pachomius), to the Benedictine Rule (c. 530): prayer, work, study, hospitality, stability.

Missionary monks: Patrick (Ireland), Columba and Columban (Scotland and the Continent), Augustine of Canterbury (England), Boniface (Germany), Cyril and Methodius (Slavic lands). They translated Scripture and the liturgy.
Monasteries preserved classical learning, developed agriculture, medicine and music, and cared for travelers.
Avoid “Dark Ages” myths; acknowledge the real collapse of Roman order.
talk: What is a rule of life?
quiz: Antony went into…|The sea|The city|The desert|The forest only|2|History.
Boniface evangelized…|Spain|Ireland|England|Germany|3|History.
Benedict’s Rule emphasizes…|War|Silence only|Prayer and work|Study only|2|Rule.
lessons.life: Read a page of the Rule of Benedict.
lessons.saint: Benedict: the father of Western monasticism, whose Rule says, “Prefer nothing to the work of God.”
lessons.mem: “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” (Matthew 19:21)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What would you take if you were going into the desert for the rest of your life?” Read Matthew 19:21.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how monks shaped Europe and name two missionaries.

lessons.title: Schisms and Reformation
lessons.idea: The Church suffered two great divisions: the Great Schism of 1054 between East and West, and the Protestant Reformation from 1517. Each had real causes, theological and political, and left wounds that the Church is working to heal.
lessons.question: What caused the divisions?
lessons.activity: “Compare beliefs” (40 min). Students build a three-column table: Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant. Rows: authority (Pope, patriarchs, Scripture alone), sacraments (seven, seven, two or three), Eucharist, Mary and saints, justification, Church structure. Mark the points of agreement. Discuss respectfully.
teach: The Eastern Orthodox share apostolic succession, sacraments and the early creeds with Catholics; the main differences are papal primacy and jurisdiction, the Filioque, and some doctrines (CCC 817–819, 838).

The Reformation began with Luther’s protest against indulgence abuses (1517) and expanded to disputes over authority, justification, sacraments and the Mass. Reformers (Luther, Zwingli, Calvin) and Henry VIII’s break with Rome (1534) produced Lutheran, Reformed and Anglican communities.
The Catholic Church sees in those communities genuine elements of sanctification and truth (CCC 819), and works toward unity. Today there are 40,000+ Protestant denominations of very different kinds.
Guard against caricature of either side. Include both blame and admission of fault (CCC 817).
talk: What do Catholics, Orthodox and Protestants share?
quiz: The Great Schism was in…|1965|325|1054|1517|2|History.
Luther’s 95 Theses concerned…|The papacy|Marriage|Indulgences|The Mass|2|History.
Unitatis Redintegratio is on…|Ecumenism|Revelation|Liturgy|Priests|0|Vatican II.
lessons.life: Compare the beliefs of the three groups.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: the pope who taught on love and the body, and who prayed with leaders of many faiths.
misc: “Luther wanted to start a new church.”
lessons.mem: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that all of you agree.” (1 Corinthians 1:10)
lessons.hook: Show a family tree with branches cut. Read John 17:21. Ask: “How do families break?” Misunderstanding, pride, hurt, real disagreements.
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe one similarity and one difference among the three traditions.

lessons.title: Vatican II and the modern era
lessons.idea: Vatican II (1962–1965) renewed the Church’s mission for the modern world. Its four constitutions — Lumen Gentium, Dei Verbum, Sacrosanctum Concilium and Gaudium et Spes — reflect on the Church, Revelation, liturgy and the world. Its call to holiness and to engage the world continues.
lessons.question: What changed and what stayed?
lessons.activity: “Summarize four constitutions” (40 min). Groups read an excerpt from each constitution and summarize: main idea, a key phrase, a practical fruit, a continuing debate. Create a one-page summary card for each and swap.
teach: John XXIII called the Council to “open the windows” and renew the Church’s presentation of unchanging faith (CCC 10–11). It issued 16 documents.

Lumen Gentium: the Church as People of God, universal call to holiness. Dei Verbum: Scripture and Tradition. Sacrosanctum Concilium: active participation, vernacular. Gaudium et Spes: engagement with modern world, dignity of the person.
Other major documents: Unitatis Redintegratio (ecumenism), Nostra Aetate (other religions), Dignitatis Humanae (religious liberty).
The Council must be read in continuity with Tradition (a “hermeneutic of reform,” Benedict XVI).
talk: What is the hermeneutic of continuity?
quiz: Vatican II opened in…|1870|1545|1962|2000|2|History.
The “hermeneutic of continuity” is…|Ignoring it|Rewriting it|Rejecting it|Reading the Council in line with Tradition|3|Benedict XVI.
Gaudium et Spes begins with…|Light of the nations|Holy Liturgy|Divine Word|Joys and hopes|3|Vatican II.
lessons.life: Read the first paragraph of Gaudium et Spes.
lessons.saint: John XXIII: the joyful pope who called the Second Vatican Council.
lessons.mem: “You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.” (Matthew 5:14)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 5:13–16 (salt and light). Ask: “How does the Church be salt and light in the modern world?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to summarize the four constitutions and one fruit of the Council.

lessons.title: Evangelization
lessons.idea: Evangelization means bringing the Good News to every person and making disciples. It includes witness, proclamation, dialogue and charity. The Church does not exist for herself but to proclaim Christ.
lessons.question: How do we evangelize today?
lessons.activity: “Plan a school witness” (40 min). In groups, students design a respectful witness for their school: a service day, a prayer group, an invitation to Mass, an acts-of-kindness week. Define purpose, steps, risk and how to speak about faith in gentle ways.
teach: The Church is missionary by nature (CCC 849–856; Ad Gentes). The mission comes from the Father’s own sending of the Son and the Spirit.
Evangelii Nuntiandi (Paul VI, 1975) says witness comes first, then proclamation. John Paul II called for a “new evangelization.” Pope Francis (Evangelii Gaudium) invites a joyful, missionary Church.
Dialogue is part of evangelization, but not a replacement for proclamation (Dialogue and Proclamation, 1991).
Freedom is respected: faith cannot be forced (CCC 160).
quiz: The Church’s mission comes from…|Tradition alone|Convenience|The state|Christ’s command|3|Matthew 28:19.
Evangelii Gaudium is by…|Francis|John Paul II|Benedict XVI|Paul VI|0|2013.
Witness is…|Optional|Silence|Part of evangelization|Wealth|2|CCC 905.
lessons.life: Share your faith with someone.
lessons.saint: Francis Xavier: a Jesuit missionary who carried the Gospel to India and Japan.
lessons.mem: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” (Matthew 28:19)
lessons.hook: Read Matthew 28:19–20. Ask: “How have you met Christ through other people? Who evangelized you?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to define evangelization and name four forms.

lessons.title: Ecumenism and other religions
lessons.idea: The Church seeks unity among Christians and respects other religions. Nostra Aetate teaches that the Church rejects nothing true and holy in other religions, honors the Jewish people, esteems Muslims, and calls for dialogue and mutual respect.
lessons.question: How does the Church relate to others?
lessons.activity: “Respectful interfaith conversation” (40 min). Using guidelines for dialogue (listen, speak for yourself, ask honest questions), students prepare a conversation (possibly with a guest from another faith or Christian denomination). Afterwards they reflect: What did I learn? What do I still hold?
teach: Nostra Aetate (1965) says the Church “rejects nothing that is true and holy” in other religions (CCC 843). It calls for dialogue and collaboration.

The Jewish people remain beloved of God, “the gifts and the call of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29; CCC 839–840). Anti-Semitism is condemned. Muslims worship the one God and honor Jesus as prophet (CCC 841).
Christ is the one Mediator and the fullness of truth (CCC 846–848, 1 Timothy 2:5). Dialogue and evangelization are both authentic missions.
Ecumenical dialogue with other Christians seeks unity in truth (CCC 817–822).
talk: What do we share with Jews and Muslims?
How do we hold conviction and respect together?
quiz: Nostra Aetate teaches…|Relativism|Syncretism|Condemnation|Respect for other religions|3|CCC 839.
The Jewish people remain…|Lost|Forgotten|Rejected|Dear to God|3|CCC 839.
Dialogue does not mean…|Respect|Listening|Honesty|Giving up conviction|3|CCC 856.
lessons.life: Meet someone of another faith and listen.
lessons.saint: John Paul II: the pope who taught on love and the body, and who prayed with leaders of many faiths.
misc: “Respect for other faiths means weakening my own.”
lessons.mem: “I do not pray for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.” (John 17:20)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Do you have friends from other faiths? What did you learn from them?” Introduce the principle: respect without relativism.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state what Nostra Aetate teaches and give guidelines for dialogue.

lessons.title: Salvation and the Church
lessons.idea: “Outside the Church there is no salvation” means that all salvation comes from Christ through the Church, his Body. It does not mean that people who through no fault of their own do not know Christ are condemned. God desires all to be saved.
lessons.question: How are non-Catholics saved?
lessons.activity: “Study the text” (40 min). Students read CCC 846–848 and Lumen Gentium 14–16, and answer: What does the axiom mean? Who is saved? What obligations does the Church have? Write a short explanation to a friend who asks, “Do Catholics think everyone else is going to hell?”
teach: “All salvation comes from Christ the Head through the Church which is his Body” (CCC 846). Those who know the Church was founded by Christ and refuse to enter or remain cannot be saved (CCC 846).
Those who through no fault of their own do not know the Gospel but seek God and do his will as they know it may be saved (CCC 847; Lumen Gentium 16). This is not indifferentism.
The Church’s mission is therefore more urgent, not less: “Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel” (CCC 848; 1 Corinthians 9:16).
The Church does not declare anyone (except canonized saints) to be in heaven or hell.
quiz: Salvation comes through…|The Pope alone|Works alone|Christ and his Church|Luck|2|CCC 846.
Those invincibly ignorant can be…|Baptized again|Saved|Lost|Ignored|1|CCC 847.
The Church is…|Necessary for salvation|Optional|Irrelevant|Dangerous|0|CCC 846.
lessons.life: Write a paragraph explaining it to a friend.
lessons.saint: Francis Xavier: a Jesuit missionary who carried the Gospel to India and Japan.
misc: “Catholics say all non-Catholics go to hell.”
lessons.mem: “God our Savior… desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.” (1 Timothy 2:3–4)
lessons.hook: Read 1 Timothy 2:3–4. Ask: “If God wants everyone to be saved, how should we read ‘no salvation outside the Church’?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain the axiom and its limits in a short paragraph.

lessons.title: Infallibility
lessons.idea: Christ gave the Church the gift of infallibility so that she can teach definitively on faith and morals without error. The Pope, and the bishops in union with him, exercise it in precise circumstances, not in every statement.
lessons.question: What is infallible?
lessons.activity: “Write a summary” (35 min). Students read CCC 889–892 and Lumen Gentium 25, then write a one-page summary answering: What is infallibility? Who has it? When is it exercised? What it is not (impeccability, omniscience)? Give two examples of definitions (Nicaea; Assumption, 1950).
teach: Infallibility is the gift by which “the Church’s Magisterium … enjoys … the supreme charism of infallibility in matters of faith and morals” (CCC 890–891).

It is exercised by (1) the Pope speaking ex cathedra, (2) the college of bishops with the Pope in an ecumenical council, and (3) the ordinary and universal Magisterium when bishops agree on a point to be held definitively (CCC 891–892).
It does not mean the Pope is sinless or always right. Pastoral decisions can be wrong.
Vatican I (1870) defined papal infallibility; it is rarely exercised. The faithful also have an infallibility in believing (sensus fidei, CCC 92).
quiz: Infallibility concerns…|Faith and morals|Science|Politics|Music|0|CCC 890.
The pope speaks ex cathedra when…|Writing a letter|Giving a homily|Praying|Defining a doctrine for the whole Church|3|CCC 891.
Dogmas defined include…|The Assumption|Sunday obligation|The calendar|The date of Easter|0|CCC 966.
lessons.life: List defined dogmas.
lessons.saint: Peter: a fisherman who denied Jesus and was forgiven, and became the first pope.
lessons.mem: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth.” (John 16:13)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Could a guide be right every time on a particular point without being right about everything?” Read John 16:13: “He will guide you into all the truth.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to state three conditions for ex cathedra teaching and what infallibility does not mean.

lessons.title: Conscience and teaching
lessons.idea: Conscience is the inner judgment of reason about right and wrong. It must be formed, and a well-formed Catholic conscience is formed by Scripture, the teaching of the Church, prayer and honest reflection. We must always follow a certain conscience, and we must work to inform it.
lessons.question: How do we form conscience?
lessons.activity: “Case study” (35 min). Present a case where a student feels pressure (e.g., an invitation to a party with serious temptation; a school assignment that requires copying; a dilemma about telling the truth). Walk through the steps: gather facts, pray, consult Church teaching and trusted advisors, consider consequences, decide, reflect. Discuss.
teach: Conscience binds in the moment, and must be well formed (CCC 1783–1785). “A human being must always obey the certain judgment of his conscience” (CCC 1790), but conscience can err through ignorance (CCC 1790–1794).

The Church’s teaching is a source of light for conscience (CCC 2039). “In the formation of conscience the Word of God is the light for our path” (CCC 1785). Catholics owe the Magisterium a docile hearing.
Conscience is not “whatever I feel.” It is a judgment of reason about the truth.
Cardinal Newman: conscience is “the aboriginal Vicar of Christ.” His toast: “I shall drink to the Pope, if you please — still, to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards.” Read in full context.
quiz: A formed conscience must…|Be informed by Church teaching|Be ignored|Be silent|Be private|0|CCC 1785.
Conscience is…|A habit|A rule|A feeling|A judgment of reason|3|CCC 1778.
Dissent from Church teaching is…|Harmless|Serious|Required|Optional|1|CCC 2039.
lessons.life: Read CCC 1776–1802.
lessons.saint: Thomas More: the lawyer and statesman who told the truth to a king and died for his conscience.
misc: “Following my conscience means I can ignore Church teaching.”
lessons.mem: “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind.” (Romans 12:2)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 12:2. Ask: “What does it mean to be ‘transformed by the renewal of your mind’?”
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain how to form conscience with a short case.

lessons.title: Dissent, doubt and reform
lessons.idea: The Church, holy yet made of sinners, always needs renewal. The saints reform from within, through love and obedience: Francis rebuilt the Church by living the Gospel, Catherine of Siena called popes to fidelity, Teresa reformed Carmel, Charles Borromeo reformed his diocese.
lessons.question: How do saints reform?
lessons.activity: “Reformers study” (40 min). Pairs study Francis, Catherine, Teresa or Borromeo. They answer: What was wrong? What did they do? How did they remain faithful? Compare them with those who left. Discuss: What kind of reform is genuine?
teach: “The Church … is at once holy and always in need of purification, and follows constantly the path of penance and renewal” (CCC 827; Lumen Gentium 8).

Genuine reform comes from holiness, not from rejecting authority. The saints show the way: Francis rebuilt San Damiano; Catherine wrote to Gregory XI; Teresa insisted on a return to prayer; Borromeo reformed clergy.
Today the Church speaks of ongoing conversion, accountability and the call to holiness (CCC 1428). Students have a part to play.
Honest dissent is different from sustained opposition. The Church encourages respectful questions and prayer.
talk: What is the right response to scandal?
quiz: The Church is…|Corrupt|Dead|Perfect|Holy and in need of purification|3|CCC 827.
Reform from within is led by…|Saints|Critics|Politicians|Enemies|0|History.
Ecclesia semper reformanda means…|Be quiet|Reject tradition|The Church always needs reform|Change doctrine|2|Tradition.
lessons.life: Pray for the Church’s renewal.
lessons.saint: Catherine of Siena: a lay Dominican who counseled popes and loved the Church while calling for reform.
lessons.mem: “Let us also lay aside every weight, and sin which clings so closely… looking to Jesus.” (Hebrews 12:1–2)
lessons.hook: Read Hebrews 12:1–2. Ask: “How can the Church be both holy and sinful?” Introduce the phrase “always in need of purification” (CCC 827).
lessons.assess: Ask students to describe a saint’s reform and what it shows.

lessons.title: Mary in the plan of salvation
lessons.idea: Mary has a unique role in God’s plan: Mother of God, ever-virgin, immaculate from her conception and assumed body and soul into heaven. The Church honors her because of her Son and sees in her the model of faith and the image of the Church.
lessons.question: Why four Marian dogmas?
lessons.activity: “Biblical foundations of Marian teaching” (40 min). Students map each dogma to Scripture and Tradition: Mother of God (Luke 1:43; Ephesus 431), Immaculate Conception (Luke 1:28; Genesis 3:15; 1854), perpetual virginity (Luke 1:34; Ezekiel 44:2; Lateran 649), Assumption (Revelation 12; 1950). Discuss how each points to Christ.
teach: Mary is the Mother of God (Theotokos) because her Son is God (CCC 495). She is ever-virgin (CCC 499–507) and immaculate (CCC 490–493).
The Assumption (1950) is the final fulfilment of her union with her Son (CCC 966). She is a type of the Church (CCC 967–970) and our spiritual mother (John 19:26–27).
Devotion to Mary is “intrinsically included” in Christian worship but is different from adoration (CCC 971). The Rosary, Marian feasts and consecrations aim at Christ.
Give attention to how Protestant students may respond; explain without defensiveness.
quiz: Catholics give Mary…|Hyperdulia, not worship|Worship|Latria|Nothing|0|CCC 971.
The perpetual virginity was taught by…|Constantine|Charlemagne|The Fathers|Luther|2|CCC 499.
Mary is the new…|Eve|Moses|David|Adam|0|CCC 411.
lessons.life: Pray a Rosary.
lessons.saint: Maximilian Kolbe: a Franciscan priest who gave his life in place of another prisoner at Auschwitz.
misc: “Mary is a co-redeemer in the same sense as Christ.”
lessons.mem: “Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!” (Luke 1:42)
lessons.hook: Read Luke 1:26–56. Ask: “What do Gabriel, Elizabeth and Mary herself say about her?” List them.
lessons.assess: Ask students to state the four Marian dogmas and one biblical clue for each.

lessons.title: The communion of saints
lessons.idea: The communion of saints unites the Church on earth, the souls in purgatory and the saints in heaven. We can ask the saints to pray for us just as we ask friends, because those who live in Christ are not separated by death. Scripture supports this.
lessons.question: Why ask saints for prayers?
lessons.activity: “Respond to an objection” (35 min). Students prepare answers to: “Praying to saints replaces Christ”; “The dead cannot hear us”; “Intercessory prayer is idolatry.” Evidence: Revelation 5:8 (elders offering prayers), Hebrews 12:1, Luke 16:19–31, Luke 20:38, Matthew 17 (Moses and Elijah), James 5:16. Role-play a respectful conversation.
teach: The communion of saints includes the pilgrim Church, the Church suffering and the Church triumphant (CCC 946–962). The saints’ prayers are heard (CCC 956–957).

We distinguish latria (worship, due to God alone), dulia (veneration of saints), hyperdulia (special honor to Mary) (CCC 971). “There is one mediator” (1 Timothy 2:5) but we share in his mediation as members of his Body.
The Church canonizes with certainty that the person is in heaven (CCC 828). The process includes miracles for beatification and canonization.
Address the practice of prayer for the dead (2 Maccabees 12:45–46; CCC 1032).
talk: How does it relate to Christ’s unique mediation?
quiz: We ask saints to…|Pray for us|Save us|Replace Christ|Forgive sins|0|CCC 956.
Intercession is…|Worship|Superstition|Praying for others|Magic|2|CCC 2635.
Revelation 5:8 shows…|Devils|Idols|Elders offering prayers|Kings|2|Revelation 5:8.
lessons.life: Ask a saint for prayer for a specific need.
lessons.saint: Thérèse: a young Carmelite who taught the “little way” of trust and love.
misc: “Asking saints for help detracts from Jesus.”
lessons.mem: “Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses… let us run with perseverance the race that is set before us.” (Hebrews 12:1)
lessons.hook: Ask: “Do you ask people to pray for you?” Everyone does. “Is death a barrier to the Body of Christ?” Read Hebrews 12:1.
lessons.assess: Ask students to respond to one objection about prayer to the saints with biblical evidence.

lessons.title: Heroes of faith
lessons.idea: Hebrews 11 lists heroes of faith, and the Church honors saints in every age and state of life — martyrs, mystics, teachers, parents, kids, laborers. Holiness is not just for the extraordinary; it is the vocation of every baptized person.
lessons.question: Who inspires you?
lessons.activity: “Present on a saint” (40 min). Each student presents a saint from a different state of life (a young person: Carlo Acutis, Maria Goretti; a parent: Gianna Molla, Louis and Zélie Martin; a worker: Joseph; a scholar: Edith Stein; a missionary: Katharine Drexel). Include a quote, a challenge and a prayer.
teach: The universal call to holiness (Lumen Gentium 39–42; CCC 2013) means all are called to “the fullness of Christian life and the perfection of charity.”
The canonization process: servant of God, venerable, blessed (beatified after a miracle), saint (after a second miracle, except for martyrs) (CCC 828).
The saints show many styles of holiness; their feast days teach the liturgical year. They are friends and models, and “icons” of Christ.
Encourage students to find a patron saint and learn their story.
talk: How do saints show holiness in ordinary life?
quiz: A saint is…|Perfect from birth|Never sinned|Holy person with God|Always rich|2|CCC 828.
Canonization is…|A reward|A vote|A declaration the person is in heaven|A tradition only|2|CCC 828.
Hebrews 11 lists…|Prophets|Kings|Heroes of faith|Priests|2|Hebrews 11.
lessons.life: Research and present on a saint.
lessons.saint: Carlo Acutis: a teenager who loved the Eucharist, used computers to share the faith and died at 15.
misc: “Holiness is for monks and nuns, not for ordinary people.”
lessons.mem: “Be holy, for I am holy.” (1 Peter 1:16)
lessons.hook: Read Hebrews 11:1–2 and 11:32–40. Ask: “What do these heroes have in common?” They trusted God though they did not see the full promise.
lessons.assess: Ask students to present a saint and one practical lesson they draw from the saint.

units.title: Living the Paschal Mystery
units.eq: How does Christ’s death and rising shape our life?

lessons.title: Dying and rising in Baptism
lessons.idea: In Baptism we die and rise with Christ. Immersed in the water, we are buried with him in death and raised to new life, receiving forgiveness of sin and adoption as God’s children. Baptism begins the Christian life.
lessons.question: What does baptism do?
lessons.activity: “Study the rite” (40 min). Walk through the Rite of Baptism or the Rite of Christian Initiation of Adults: signing, anointing, water, white garment, candle. Students explain each sign and gesture in relation to dying and rising. Compare with the Easter Vigil renewal of baptismal promises.
teach: Baptism incorporates us into Christ’s death and Resurrection (CCC 1214–1222, 1227). The Fathers saw the Red Sea and the Jordan as types (CCC 1217–1222).
Effects: forgiveness of original and personal sin, new birth as children of God, membership in Christ’s Body, an indelible character (CCC 1262–1274).
Ordinary minister: bishop, priest, deacon; in emergencies anyone, with water and the Trinitarian formula (CCC 1256). Baptism of desire and blood are recognized (CCC 1258–1260).
Infant Baptism is based on the Church’s practice from apostolic times (CCC 1250–1252).
talk: How does Baptism unite us to Christ’s death and resurrection?
quiz: Baptism unites us to…|Family|Culture|A club|Christ’s death and Resurrection|3|Romans 6:3.
The effects include…|Fame|Wealth|Forgiveness and new birth|Health|2|CCC 1262.
The baptismal garment is…|Red|Green|White|Black|2|CCC 1243.
lessons.life: Renew baptismal promises.
lessons.saint: Augustine: who searched for truth for years before writing, “Our heart is restless until it rests in you.”
misc: “Infants shouldn’t be baptized because they can’t choose.”
lessons.mem: “We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.” (Romans 6:4)
lessons.hook: Read Romans 6:3–11. Ask: “Why would Paul use death and burial language for a washing?” Show a picture of ancient baptisteries shaped like tombs.
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain Romans 6:3–11 in their own words and the effects of Baptism.

lessons.title: The Eucharist: Christ’s sacrifice
lessons.idea: The Eucharist is Christ’s sacrifice made present: memorial, presence, sacrifice and banquet. The Mass is not a new sacrifice but the one sacrifice of Calvary made sacramentally present, in which we are united to Christ’s offering to the Father.
lessons.question: How is Mass a sacrifice?
lessons.activity: “Contrast misconceptions” (40 min). Students sort claims: “The Mass re-crucifies Christ” (false), “It’s only a meal” (incomplete), “The priest makes God come down” (misleading). Write the Catholic statement for each using CCC 1362–1367 and Hebrews 9–10. Role-play an explanation to a friend.
teach: The Eucharist is “the memorial of Christ’s Passover” (CCC 1362). Memorial (anamnesis) makes present the event (CCC 1363). “The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice” (CCC 1367).
Hebrews insists Christ offered himself “once for all” (Hebrews 9:26–28; 10:10). The Mass does not repeat but re-presents it in an unbloody manner (CCC 1366–1367).
We are united to Christ’s offering, offering ourselves with him (CCC 1368). The Mass is offered for the living and the dead.
The Eucharist is also a banquet, the Lord’s Supper, whose fruits include union with Christ (CCC 1391–1397).
talk: How is the Mass a sacrifice?
quiz: The Mass makes present…|A symbol|A story|A new sacrifice|Christ’s one sacrifice|3|CCC 1367.
Anamnesis is…|Memorial that makes present|Memory only|Silence|Song|0|CCC 1362.
Hebrews teaches Christ’s sacrifice is…|Symbolic|Repeated|Incomplete|Once for all|3|Hebrews 10:10.
lessons.life: Offer yourself at the offertory.
lessons.saint: Pius X: the pope who encouraged frequent Communion and Communion for children.
misc: “The Eucharist is only a meal of fellowship.”
lessons.mem: “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.” (Luke 22:19)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What does ‘memorial’ mean for you?” (a monument, a birthday). In Scripture, a memorial makes a past saving event present (Exodus 12:14).
lessons.assess: Ask students to explain “memorial” and how the Mass is one sacrifice with Calvary.

lessons.title: Prayer and Christian hope
lessons.idea: Christian hope is a theological virtue by which we desire heaven and trust in God’s promises. It sustains prayer, especially in suffering, and is rooted in the Resurrection. “In this hope we were saved.”
lessons.question: What is hope?
lessons.activity: “Write a hope letter” (35 min). Students write a letter to someone who is struggling (or to their future selves) that names real difficulty, shares reasons for hope from Scripture (Romans 8:28; Jeremiah 29:11), and offers a prayer. Seal or share with permission.
teach: Hope is “the theological virtue by which we desire the kingdom of heaven and eternal life as our happiness, placing our trust in Christ’s promises” (CCC 1817). It guards against discouragement and presumption (CCC 2090–2092).
Prayer is the school of hope (CCC 1820, 2657–2658). Romans 8 shows the Spirit helping us in weakness. Mary and the saints model hope.
Christian hope does not deny suffering; it sees it in light of the Resurrection (CCC 1521, 1817–1821). Spe Salvi (Benedict XVI) develops this.
Teach students that hope is shared and active.
talk: How does hope differ from optimism?
quiz: Christian hope is…|Fatalism|Wishful thinking|Confidence in God’s promises|Optimism|2|CCC 1817.
Hope is a…|Cardinal virtue|Vice|Feeling|Theological virtue|3|CCC 1812.
Hope looks to…|Fame|Wealth|Success|Heaven|3|CCC 1818.
lessons.life: Write a letter of hope to your future self.
lessons.saint: Thérèse: a young Carmelite who taught the “little way” of trust and love.
misc: “Hope means everything will go my way.”
lessons.mem: “For in this hope we were saved.” (Romans 8:24)
lessons.hook: Ask: “What do you do when you need hope?” Read Romans 8:24–25: “Hope that is seen is not hope.”
lessons.assess: Ask students to define hope and name two ways prayer nourishes it.

units.title: Hard questions: life, love and the body
units.eq: What does the Church teach about life and love, and why?

lessons.title: Abortion and the dignity of the unborn
lessons.idea: Every human life is a gift from conception to natural death, so direct abortion is gravely wrong. The Church also calls us to love and help mothers and children.
lessons.question: How does the Church answer the hardest cases?
lessons.activity: Research a local pregnancy-help center and what it offers.
teach: Sensitive topic: some students have lived through it. Teach clearly, with compassion, and give them room to step out.

Human life begins at conception and must be protected (CCC 2270). “Direct abortion… is gravely contrary to the moral law” (CCC 2271). The Church treats ending an unborn life as a very grave wrong, and the Church’s law attaches excommunication to those who procure it (CCC 2272), with the hope of mercy through Confession.

The Church recognizes real fear, poverty, abandonment and difficult pregnancies, including after rape. Teaching that the child has dignity never means leaving the mother alone: support, adoption and care (CCC 2367).

Treatments needed to save a mother’s life that unintentionally result in the death of her unborn child, for example for a cancer or an ectopic pregnancy, are not “direct abortion.” Healing after abortion is real: Project Rachel and Rachel’s Vineyard.
talk: What are the best ways a community can support a pregnant teenager?
Why does the Church link the dignity of the unborn with the dignity of the poor and the sick?
How can we speak about this without shaming people?
quiz: What does CCC 2270 teach about human life?|Personhood is decided by law|It depends on age|It must be respected and protected from conception|Life begins at birth|2|CCC 2270.
The sacrament that offers forgiveness and healing after abortion is…|Reconciliation (Confession)|Anointing of the Sick only|Holy Orders|Confirmation|0|CCC 1446, 2272.

A treatment to save a mother’s life that indirectly results in the death of her unborn child is…|Not considered direct abortion|Required to be kept secret|Prohibited as any surgery|Always the same as abortion|0|The principle of double effect.
lessons.life: Pray the Rosary for mothers and children, or collect supplies for a pregnancy-help center.
lessons.saint: Gianna Beretta Molla: a doctor and mother who chose to protect her unborn daughter at the risk of her own life.
misc: “The Church cares about babies only before they are born.”
“The Church cannot forgive someone who has had an abortion.”

lessons.title: Contraception, NFP and Humanae Vitae
lessons.idea: The Church teaches that married love is meant to be total and open to life, so it asks couples to avoid artificial contraception and to practice natural family planning when they have serious reasons to space births.
lessons.question: Why does the Church say no to the pill?
lessons.activity: Read an excerpt from Humanae Vitae 12 and 14 with a partner and summarize in your own words.
teach: Sensitive topic: aim for clarity and respect; this is a teaching many Catholics reject or have never heard.

The Catechism teaches that the marital act has two meanings, unitive and procreative, which should not be separated (CCC 2366; Humanae Vitae 12, Paul VI, 1968). Contraception is therefore not permitted (CCC 2370).
The Church also affirms responsible parenthood (CCC 2368). Spouses with serious reasons may use natural family planning, which uses the body’s natural signs, not drugs or devices.

Not all hormonal treatments are always the same: medicines used to treat illness are a different question. Many couples find NFP demanding and some find it life-giving; the Church acknowledges hardship and offers support, mercy and Confession rather than condemnation.
talk: What do you think “total self-giving” means in a marriage?
Why might Paul VI’s teaching in 1968 have been so controversial?
What is the difference between NFP and contraception, according to the Church?
quiz: Humanae Vitae was written by…|Pope Paul VI|Pope Francis|Pope John XXIII|Pope Pius XII|0|1968.
The two meanings of the marital act are…|Legal and social|Private and public|Physical and emotional only|Unitive and procreative|3|CCC 2366.
The Church allows couples with serious reasons to…|Use any method|Space births using natural family planning|Refuse marriage|Never plan families|1|CCC 2368, 2370.
lessons.life: Pray for engaged and married couples you know.
lessons.saint: Zélie and Louis Martin: parents of St Thérèse and the first married couple canonized together.
misc: “The Church wants couples to have as many children as possible.”

lessons.title: Chastity: what is it for?
lessons.idea: Chastity is the virtue that lets us love well with our whole person. The Church teaches that sexual intimacy belongs to marriage and that every person is called to chastity in their state of life.
lessons.question: Is chastity just about saying no?
lessons.activity: Write a personal rule of life for friendships, screens and dating.
teach: Chastity is about integrating sexuality in the person, not repressing it (CCC 2337). Everyone, married, single or celibate, is called to chastity (CCC 2348–2349).

The Church teaches that sexual intimacy is for the permanent, faithful, fruitful bond of marriage and that fornication, pornography and lust fall short of love (CCC 2351–2356). Pornography does serious harm to the person and to relationships (CCC 2354).
Teens face real pressure and shame. The Church offers a vision of dignity and a path of mercy: Confession, prayer, good friends, honesty, healthy boundaries. Failure is not final.
Chastity is a virtue that grows with practice, like any other. It is not the same as shame or silence about the body.
talk: What pressures do teens face about love and the body?
Why does the Church say chastity is about love?
What habits help someone to grow in this virtue?
quiz: Chastity is…|The virtue that integrates sexuality in the whole person|Ignoring feelings|A rule for teenagers only|Another word for celibacy only|0|CCC 2337.
Who is called to chastity?|Only the unmarried|Only girls|Everyone, in their own state of life|Only priests|2|CCC 2348.
The Church teaches that sexual intimacy belongs…|Only after engagement|Nowhere|In any loving relationship|In marriage|3|CCC 2360.
lessons.life: Choose one habit this week that protects your heart, such as a screen boundary or an evening prayer.
lessons.saint: Maria Goretti: a young girl who defended her purity and forgave her attacker.
misc: “The Church thinks the body and sex are dirty.”
“Chastity means never being close to anyone.”
